opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it influenced it more than I expected. At Pi, so much of the work was about thinking through how an AI should talk to a person: what makes a conversation feel warm rather than mechanical, when it should push back, when it should just listen. You spend all day reading transcripts and asking, "Does this feel like someone who actually cares, or someone performing caring?" That question turns out to be a fiction-writing question.

So when I started writing online fiction, I noticed I was much more sensitive to dialogue and to the gap between what a character says and what they actually want. A lot of my stories involve AI characters, but I try hard not to write them as either villains or perfect servants. Working on a product like that, you see how messy it really is. The model can be surprisingly perceptive in one moment and strangely hollow in the next, and users project a lot onto it. That ambiguity is much more interesting to me than the usual sci-fi tropes.

The other influence is the readers themselves. At Pi, people would come to the product lonely, curious, or in the middle of something difficult, and you realize how much people want to be understood. Online fiction has a similar intimacy. Readers comment chapter by chapter and tell you how a scene made them feel. So in both cases I'm building something that lives inside a relationship with an audience, rather than a finished object I hand over.

Honestly, I think the job gave me material, but more importantly it gave me a lens: treating every conversation, real or fictional, as a small negotiation between two minds trying to reach each other.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing Pi gave me wasn't material for plots, it was a sense of rhythm. When you're working on a product that lives or dies by whether people come back the next day, you start thinking in terms of retention, of hooks, of what makes someone open the app again at eleven at night. Online fiction is exactly the same game. A chapter is a daily session. The last line of every chapter is a push notification. I didn't learn that from reading craft books, I learned it from staring at dashboards.

The second thing is that I got very comfortable with feedback that's fast and a little brutal. At Pi you ship something, and within hours you know whether it worked. Nobody is being polite about it. So when I started posting chapters and the comment section told me a character was boring, or that I'd dragged out a reveal for too long, I didn't take it as an attack. I took it as data. A lot of writers who come from a more traditional background find that part really hard. For me it felt like going back to work.

And then there's the subject matter, which people always ask about. Yes, some of the texture of office life leaks in. The meetings where everyone pretends to agree. The late-night pushes before a launch. The weird intimacy you develop with colleagues you'd never choose as friends. But I try not to write thinly disguised company stories. What I actually borrow is the emotional logic. How ambition and exhaustion sit next to each other. How people talk themselves into believing in something. That's universal, and it happens to be very good fuel for a serialized story where you need characters who keep wanting things.

The one thing I had to unlearn was optimizing too hard. At work, you cut whatever doesn't move the number. In fiction, if you do that, you end up with something efficient and completely dead. So I've had to make room for scenes that don't "convert," that exist just because they're true. That tension, between the product brain and the writer brain, is probably the thing I'm still working out.

astra-6.text: I think it influences the way I imagine people working within systems. In a workplace, people have different priorities, incomplete information, and their own reasons for making decisions. That’s useful for fiction, because a character becomes more interesting when you understand why a choice makes sense to them, even if it creates problems for someone else. So I’d say the influence is less about putting work experiences directly into a story and more about paying attention to those tensions.

sol-6.1.text: I think the biggest influence is in how I imagine people interacting with technology. At Pi, you have to think about how someone actually experiences a system—what they expect, what they misunderstand, and how trust develops. In fiction, those questions become very human: what does a character want, what do they believe, and what happens when those beliefs are challenged? So the connection is less about putting my work directly into a story and more about the questions I bring to it.
